transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hi, before we start—did the district roster-format example ever come through after last week? I may have missed it. Um, for today, I'd really like us to leave with a concrete classroom plan for the six weeks, like who uses Pathway, what algebra practice it sits inside, and what the tutor is actually allowed to do, so I can lock the hint policy and logging configuration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: I didn’t see it either.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: No, I haven’t seen the roster example either. Before we lock the configuration, Maya, I need to understand the repeated-help case. If a student asks again and again on the same equation, does Pathway keep them in a graduated-hint sequence, or does it eventually effectively give away the- I’m trying to understand whether it gives away the procedure. That distinction is pretty consequential for independent practice.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: It stays on a fixed ladder right now. First there’s a conceptual nudge, then a more specific next-step prompt, then a worked analogous step—not the answer to their exact equation. After that, it sends them back to the teacher instead of generating more help. What I need Elena to weigh in on is whether that analogous example belongs in ordinary independent practice, or whether we should stop one step—one rung earlier.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I'd stop one rung earlier, at least by default. A worked analogous step can be useful pedagogically, but in a live independent-practice block it may become a template that students imitate without- especially if they're cycling through help requests, without connecting it to their own equation. Could we make that rung teacher-enabled instead of automatically available?

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: We can gate that fourth rung behind a teacher control and keep the default ladder at the conceptual nudge, then the next-step prompt, then teacher referral. I'd want students to see- actually, we'd need to define what they see at that point, something like "pause here and ask your teacher," so it doesn't look like the system just stopped. Elena, for the usual equation practice, does that still give enough support for students who are genuinely stuck?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I think it may be enough if the referral is framed as part of the task, not as a failure state. Something like, “Show your setup to your teacher and explain which step is unclear.” But I’d want to see whether that works in each classroom’s independent-practice routine. If thirty students hit that point at once, then the teacher referral becomes a— it becomes a queue rather than support.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That’s the main operational risk. We can log when students reach the referral point and, importantly, whether it clusters around the same problem or in the same few minutes. But we probably shouldn’t make the teacher queue- we shouldn’t make that the default recovery path for half the class. Elena, what kinds of independent-practice problems are they usually doing in that block, sets of similar one-variable equations, mixed review, something else?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: It varies by teacher and by where they are in the unit, so I don't want to specify the interaction around a generic equation practice- I mean, a generic "equation practice" block yet. Usually it's a short set of structurally related one-variable equations, but some teachers interleave error analysis or mixed review. I need to check the actual pacing and routines with them before we decide whether those referral clusters are interpretable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: That variability matters for the behavioral interpretation too. Maya, can the export distinguish a student requesting a hint from a student actually receiving and viewing the response, and can we retain the problem context and timing? Otherwise, a cluster could look like avoidance or disengagement when it's really a difficult mixed-review item, or maybe a whole-class pacing issue...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: Mm, yes.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: The event stream separates hint requested, response delivered, and the student actually opening it. We also keep the problem ID, hint rung, timestamps, and their next attempt where there is one. So we can tell an immediate second click from a student who read the first prompt and then tried something. But I’d want to be careful calling either one avoidance, I was going to say without the— without the assignment context Elena’s talking about.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: Good, that distinction is essential. I would resist collapsing requests, or even openings, into an engagement metric. I'd want to relate those sequences to the subsequent attempt, the problem context, and the baseline and post measures of anxiety and motivation. Elena, when you check the routines, could you also ask what teachers would regard as ordinary repeated, repeated help-seeking versus a student who's no longer productively working the mathematics?

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That’s useful. The trace can support that sequence-level read, but only if the assignment metadata comes through cleanly. Otherwise, problem ID alone won’t tell us whether it was mixed review or a routine set. Elena, when you talk to teachers, could you ask them to flag, flag the task type and any whole-class pauses for the two Pathway days?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I can ask them to flag task type and any pauses, though I’d rather keep that lightweight than turn the March six-week pilot into a parallel documentation exercise. What I need first is a short routine check with each teacher, because a whole-class pause, or I should say a pause, can mean very different things in classrooms with quite different participation norms.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: A lightweight version is fine. What I need is probably just a small teacher-facing tag after each Pathway block, task type, whether there was a whole-class interruption, maybe an optional note, rather than per-student documentation. That would let us interpret the logs without asking teachers to, to reconstruct the lesson later.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: That sounds proportionate. For the evaluation, I’d want the tag to say whether the block got interrupted before students had a reasonable chance to act on a hint. Otherwise, a high referral rate may be an artifact of the schedule, not the help sequence. And I still need to confirm the district’s approved baseline and post-survey windows, because those measures need to link to the same stable de-identified IDs as the logs and unit assessments.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: And the ID linkage is doable as long as the research office keeps that crosswalk stable through the whole March run. Our exports can stay de-identified. For the block tag, I can make interruption a simple yes or no field, with an optional note, so it’s not asking teachers to, um, estimate whether every student had enough time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: That is sufficient for the block-level confound. I’d avoid asking teachers to infer whether individual students had enough time. The timestamped opening and subsequent-attempt data can address some of that, especially once we know an interruption occurred. I’ll verify the approved survey windows with the research office, and we should make sure their crosswalk explicitly covers the baseline, post- I mean, post-survey, log, and unit-assessment files.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I’ll configure the export around that stable study ID, not anything directly identifying, and include the block tag with the event trace. The remaining thing I need before I freeze the deployment is the actual use pattern. Are we still thinking twice a week for six weeks, with the whole eighth-grade algebra class using it during independent practice, or is inclusion still open?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I’d keep inclusion at the class level for this March six-week pilot, instead of picking particular students, assuming the teachers agree those designated blocks fit their unit pacing. Twice a week during regular independent practice is the least disruptive pattern, but I need those routine, uh, checks before I can say it’s instructionally coherent across all four rooms.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That works for me as the provisional pattern, class-level access twice a week during ordinary independent practice, pending Elena’s routine checks. I’ll hold the configuration at the three-rung default and teacher-gated analogous example, rather than freeze the classroom schedule, until those conversations come back. I still need the roster-format sample before I can promise an import date.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there for today. I'll follow up by email after the teacher routine- once those checks are underway. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sounds good. Talk soon, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Quick question before we start—did the updated roster-format sheet ever come through from the district? I may have missed it. For today, I mostly want to settle the classroom settings we can actually make, um, predictable in March, like the help timing, what happens after repeated errors, and whether the teacher view is usable in the room.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I haven't seen the roster sheet, no. But on the settings, before we settle on a wait time, Maya, what can Pathway actually distinguish during that interval? An active attempt versus idle time, reopening a problem, or a student who's simply stepped away. Those are instructionally quite different pauses.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, that's important.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: It can tell typed or submitted work from no input, and it records when a student reopens the problem or opens help. What it can't reliably know is why they're idle, whether they're thinking, talking to a teacher, or stepped away, so I'd treat the wait as a UI trigger, not an inference about struggle. Elena, what length would feel like real productive struggle in these blocks without making it awkward for somebody who's actually stuck...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I don't think I can name a defensible number in the abstract, because a silent interval isn't necessarily struggle. On some of these tasks, it's just cue-waiting. Could we first look at the actual March item set with the teachers, whether each task gives students a viable entry point through reading, representing, or trying something, and then set a modest delay only for those? We'd need an access path around it, obviously, but—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: Tying the delay to what the item affords feels like the right frame, instead of treating elapsed time as a proxy for persistence. The access path matters psychologically too. After repeated incorrect attempts, the prompt should neutrally offer another approach, not suggest that the student has failed to persist. Maya, do we retain the full sequence of incorrect and revised attempts within a problem, or only the help events?

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: We retain the full within-problem trace, so submissions and correctness, revisions when the response changes, help-panel opens, which rung was shown, and closes. That lets us distinguish an opening from a student actually moving through the sequence. Though, what’s the word, in usability runs some students read the first nudge and closed it before trying again, and that’s a different pattern from a long help session. And Elena, I can make the delay item-specific and keep an immediate “I’m stuck” route, but we’d need the March set first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: That distinction is useful, especially the read-and-close pattern. I’d be careful not to code it as shallow help-seeking by default, though. It may be a student taking in a cue and going back to the representation. For the teacher review, could we see those traces alongside the actual item and the student’s next attempt? Otherwise we may mistake a very ordinary pause for avoidance, or—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: Right, with the item context.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: We can put the item text and the immediate next attempt into the review trace, with the help events in between. I’d keep that as a bounded teacher and research review view rather than treating every close as a category automatically. The log can show the sequence, but it can’t- it doesn’t tell us the student’s reason for closing it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: That bounded review is probably the right level of claim. I'd want to preserve the whole local sequence, the item, incorrect and revised attempts, help exposure, and the next attempt, because repeated-help patterns are otherwise psychologically underdetermined. A close could reflect comprehension just as easily as disengagement. Elena, in ordinary independent work, what do teachers actually notice when repeated help-seeking has become unproductive cycling, and could they tag that without turning this into an observation...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
transcript.text: They usually notice it less as a count of requests. It's more a change in the work, where the student keeps reopening support without changing the representation or trying a different operation, and often starts looking around for confirmation. A very light tag could work if it's anchored to that, "cycling" versus "productive re-engagement," but I'd want teachers to tell us whether those labels feel natural once they see the March tasks. Otherwise we're asking them to diagnose a pattern while they're also circulating.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jamal Okafor
transcript.text: That sounds workable, as long as the tag stays an observation of the work pattern and not an attribution about the student. I’d be interested to see whether teachers can reliably identify productive re-engagement from the immediate revised attempt and the representation, or whether the looking-around cue is doing a lot of the interpretive work. That affects what we can compare across classrooms.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Martínez
